patient.name: Priya Nakamura
patient.chiefComplaint: Severe shortness of breath, known asthmatic, not improving with home treatment

history.hpi: Patient has a known history of severe, poorly controlled asthma with a prior ICU admission and intubation two years ago. Symptoms began roughly 90 minutes ago with progressive wheezing and chest tightness; she used her home albuterol inhaler repeatedly without relief before her partner called 911. On EMS arrival she is tripod, using accessory muscles, and unable to speak more than one or two words at a time. Field bronchodilators and CPAP have been attempted en route with minimal improvement.
pastMedical: Prior ICU admission and intubation for asthma (2 years ago)
history.lastOralIntake: Coffee approximately 3 hours prior to symptom onset
history.events: Progressive wheezing and dyspnea over 90 minutes despite repeated home rescue inhaler use; partner called 911 when she could no longer speak in full sentences

scene.location: Second-floor apartment bedroom, patient seated on the edge of the bed
scene.safety: No hazards to crew; narrow stairwell noted for extrication planning
scene.bystanders: Partner present, reports repeated rescue inhaler use over the last hour with no improvement
visualCues: Patient in tripod position, visible accessory muscle use and intercostal retractions
Minimal audible air movement despite obvious work of breathing
Empty albuterol inhaler canister on the nightstand
Unable to complete a sentence, speaking one word at a time

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew finds a 32-year-old female with known severe asthma in tripod position with minimal air movement despite obvious severe work of breathing. CPAP and nebulized bronchodilators have already been trialed with little effect.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but severely compromised air movement; on CPAP with in-line nebulizer
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Severe accessory muscle use, minimal audible air movement, near-silent chest on auscultation
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, tachycardic, skin pale and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Intact, patient rigidly upright in tripod position
otherFindings: Unable to speak more than one word at a time
Near-silent chest despite visible severe distress
CPAP and nebulized albuterol/ipratropium already trialed with minimal improvement
Diaphoretic, visibly exhausted from work of breathing

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize impending respiratory failure: minimal air movement, silent chest, rising EtCO2 despite tachypnea
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Normal EtCO2 (35–45 mmHg) with tachypnea and respiratory distress is an indicator of impending respiratory failure
expectedActions.rationale: Silent chest and normalizing EtCO2 despite severe tachypnea are late, ominous signs of impending arrest, not improvement.

expectedActions.shortAction: Maintain CPAP with in-line nebulizer; do not break the mask seal
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: DO NOT discontinue CPAP/BiPAP until patient is on the emergency department stretcher and hospital CPAP/BiPAP is immediately available for patient to be switched over, or physician is at bedside and requesting CPAP/BiPAP be discontinued. Breaking the mask seal causes a significant decrease in airway pressures and may lead to abrupt decompensation due to atelectasis and alveolar collapse.
expectedActions.rationale: Breaking the seal even briefly can precipitate abrupt decompensation in a patient this tenuous.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply continuous waveform capnography; monitor for shark-fin pattern and trend EtCO2
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: A "shark fin" on waveform capnography suggests significant bronchospasm and obstructive physiology
expectedActions.rationale: Continuous capnography trending guides whether therapy is working or the patient is progressing to failure.

expectedActions.shortAction: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM (65 kg × 0.01 mg/kg = 0.65 mg → capped at 0.3 mg max)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL solution IM, maximum dose of 0.3 mg) should only be administered for impending respiratory failure as adjunctive therapy when there are no clinical signs of improvement with the above treatments
expectedActions.rationale: Adjunctive IM epinephrine is indicated once bronchodilators and NIV alone fail to reverse impending respiratory failure.

expectedActions.shortAction: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV (65 kg × 40 mg/kg = 2,600 mg → capped at 2 g max) over 10–15 minutes
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Magnesium sulfate (40 mg/kg IV, maximum dose of 2 g) over 10–15 minutes should be administered for severe bronchoconstriction and concern for impending respiratory failure
expectedActions.rationale: Magnesium provides additional smooth muscle relaxation in severe bronchoconstriction unresponsive to first-line therapy.

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes impending respiratory failure (minimal air movement, silent chest, rising/normal EtCO2 despite tachypnea) and escalates with IM epinephrine and IV magnesium sulfate as adjunctive therapy since CPAP and nebulizers alone are not sufficient.
Crew continues CPAP and nebulizer therapy alone without escalating to IM epinephrine or magnesium sulfate; the patient continues to deteriorate toward respiratory failure.

phases.name: IM epi and mag given
phases.description: Crew escalates therapy with IM epinephrine and IV magnesium sulfate while maintaining CPAP with in-line nebulized bronchodilators, continuously monitoring waveform capnography for a shark-fin pattern.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing signs of impending respiratory failure despite ongoing CPAP and nebulized bronchodilators, the crew administers weight-based IM epinephrine and IV magnesium sulfate as adjunctive therapy per protocol.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, maintained on CPAP with in-line nebulizer, mask seal maintained continuously
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Still severe accessory muscle use, air movement beginning to improve slightly, faint wheeze now audible
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, tachycardic from epinephrine effect, skin still diaphoretic
otherFindings: Faint wheeze now audible where chest was previously silent
CPAP mask seal maintained continuously, not broken
Waveform capnography shows persistent shark-fin morphology, EtCO2 trending down slightly

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue serial reassessment of air movement, EtCO2, and mental status en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Ongoing assessment is critical when an airway device is in place.
expectedActions.rationale: Status asthmaticus can relapse; continuous reassessment ensures early recognition if the patient begins to deteriorate again.

transitions.condition: Following IM epinephrine and IV magnesium sulfate, air movement and wheeze audibly improve, EtCO2 begins trending down toward normal, and mental status remains intact, avoiding the need for intubation.

phases.name: Improved, avoided intubation
phases.description: Air movement and wheeze continue to improve following adjunctive IM epinephrine and magnesium sulfate. The patient remains on CPAP with in-line nebulizer for transport, avoiding the need for RSI.
phases.triggerCondition: After IM epinephrine and IV magnesium sulfate, air movement improves, wheezing becomes more audible (a positive sign compared to the earlier silent chest), and EtCO2 trends down toward normal while mental status remains intact.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, maintained on CPAP with in-line nebulizer
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improved air movement, audible expiratory wheeze throughout, decreased accessory muscle use
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, tachycardia improving, skin warm and less diaphoretic
otherFindings: Now able to speak in short phrases
Wheeze audible throughout both lung fields, no longer silent
EtCO2 trending toward normal range, waveform shark-fin less pronounced
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I can breathe a little easier now."

phases.name: RSI performed for respiratory failure
phases.description: Despite CPAP and nebulized bronchodilators, escalation to IM epinephrine and magnesium sulfate is delayed. The patient progresses to frank respiratory failure with a silent chest and declining mental status, requiring RSI for advanced airway control.
phases.triggerCondition: Escalation to IM epinephrine and IV magnesium sulfate is delayed while the patient remains on CPAP and nebulizer alone; air movement continues to worsen with a persistently silent chest, EtCO2 rises further, and mental status declines, prompting RSI for impending respiratory failure.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Advanced airway placed via RSI; endotracheal tube confirmed with waveform capnography
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Manually ventilated at 10-12 breaths/min, bilateral breath sounds present but diminished with persistent wheeze
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, tachycardic, skin pale
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Sedated and paralyzed, no purposeful movement
otherFindings: Endotracheal tube secured, depth confirmed and documented
Waveform capnography confirms placement, persistent shark-fin morphology reflects ongoing severe bronchospasm
Ventilated with just enough volume to see chest rise, avoiding overventilation

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize progression to respiratory failure: silent chest, declining mental status, rising EtCO2
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Severe respiratory distress may manifest with hypoxia, altered mentation, diaphoresis, or inability to speak more than 2–3 words
expectedActions.rationale: Continued deterioration on CPAP/nebulizer alone without escalation signals the need for advanced airway management.

expectedActions.shortAction: Preoxygenate with high-flow O2 and positive pressure ventilation for at least 2 minutes before RSI
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient should be pre-oxygenated with high flow oxygen, and positive pressure ventilation for a minimum of two minutes prior to the procedure
expectedActions.rationale: Adequate preoxygenation limits the risk of peri-intubation hypoxia in an already compromised patient.

expectedActions.shortAction: Ketamine 98 mg IV (65 kg × 1.5 mg/kg = 97.5 mg) induction, then Rocuronium 65 mg IV (65 kg × 1 mg/kg) for paralysis
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer induction sedative agent: Etomidate IV push, 0.2-0.3 mg/kg OR Ketamine IV push, 1-2 mg/kg OR Midazolam IV push, 0.05-0.10 mg/kg ... Administer paralytic agent: Succinylcholine IV push, 1-2 mg/kg OR Rocuronium IV push, 1 mg/kg OR Vecuronium IV push, 0.1 mg/kg
expectedActions.rationale: Weight-based induction and paralysis per protocol optimize first-pass success for RSI.

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm ETT placement with waveform capnography and bilateral breath sounds, then secure the tube
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Confirm placement of advanced airway (endotracheal tube, SGA) with waveform capnography (most reliable), absent gastric sounds, and bilateral breath sounds. Secure tube manually. Once proper position is confirmed, secure the tube with tape, twill, or commercial device
expectedActions.rationale: Waveform capnography is the most reliable confirmation method and must be documented before securing the tube.
